results.title: Top 10 GTM Mistakes Founders Are Making Today with SaaStr CEO Jason Lemkin | SaaStrAI
results.content:
## Mistake #7: Hiring the Broken, the Bitter, the Fractional

The world has really changed since March 2020. For some folks today, it’s the hardest it’s ever been. Some SaaS leaders with hundreds of millions of revenue are growing at 0%. Others are more similar to 2018 when budgets had to be earned.

This has led to a lot of folks who are broken, bitter, and fractional. Folks who don’t want to do it anymore. You can’t hire anyone that won’t play the entire game. It’s too hard today.

They can’t be too angry at their last boss, think the system is loaded against them, believe that VCs are destroying people with their liquidation preferences, or think that the CEO is a terrible human being. [...] #### The Top 10 Don’ts When it Comes to GTM

1. Don’t hire a VP of Sales that can’t sell or demo the product
2. Don’t hire a VP of Marketing that can’t do demand generation
3. As a founder, don’t step out of sales too early
4. Don’t cut marketing too much, or too early
5. Don’t ignore the adoption of AI into your business
6. Don’t putting profitability above growth
7. Don’t hire the broken, the bitter, the fractional if they’re not willing to play the game
8. Don’t hire for the logo if their resume can’t back it up
9. Don’t look for Instant ROI
10. Don’t eliminate true customer success

results.content:
View profile for Dale Zwizinski

I knew go-to-market was broken in 1999. Not 2019. 1999.
Y2K, New York City, coding SQL on-site for a publishing software client. The customer told me she never wanted to see our salesperson in her office again. All he cared about was his commission.
That was the moment. The customer was sold one thing and delivered another, and the person paying the price was standing in front of me. Twenty-five years later, most GTM problems are still that same gap between what sales promises and what actually gets delivered.
Adam Jay and I go back to the origin stories, the messy version, on the latest episode of GTM Uncensored: 

### Your Startup Is Selling a Product That Doesn't Exist

#### 

🧠Vika Guseva, graphic [...] #### 

🧠Vika Guseva, graphic

The story highlights a classic issue in sales. If the salesperson is more focused on the commission than the customer’s needs, what are some practical ways to realign incentives to prioritize long-term relationships over quick wins?

LeeRon Yahalomi, graphic

The problem was never that GTM broke. It was built to reward the wrong behavior. When commission is paid at signature but the customer pays for the gap afterward, disappointment isn’t an accident. It’s the business model.

results.title: I Tell Founders to Nail Their GTM Before Scaling Their Team
results.content:
## Story That Stuck With Me

One founder I worked with raised a sizable seed round and immediately grew from 8 people to 30. The assumption was that the money was there to “go fast” The product was innovative, and the team was ambitious. But they hadn’t figured out how to consistently acquire or retain customers.

Within 12 months, half the team was gone. The burn rate was unsustainable, morale collapsed, and the founder had to reset the entire strategy. Two years later, they told me they wished they had stayed lean and focused on nailing GTM before expanding. That lesson came at the cost of millions and many broken relationships.

I’ve seen this pattern too many times to let founders I coach repeat it.

## My Thoughts [...] When that system is repeatable, measurable, and starts to feel almost boring, that’s when I say GTM is nailed. Anything earlier is still experimentation.

## The Cost of Hiring Ahead of Clarity

Hiring too early creates a dangerous illusion. A bigger team looks like progress. It feels productive to fill the office or Slack channels with new faces and new titles. But underneath, the foundation is shaky.

I’ve seen teams triple their sales headcount before a single rep had closed a deal consistently. That only magnified the uncertainty. Now instead of one person fumbling through objections, six people were fumbling at scale. Morale dropped, turnover spiked, and leadership lost confidence in the product itself. [...] ## Human Side of Scaling Too Early

Beyond wasted capital, there’s a human cost to _premature scaling_. I’ve coached teams where talented people joined with high hopes, only to burn out from the lack of direction. They weren’t failing individually, the system was failing them.

That damage lingers. Once a team experiences dysfunction at scale, trust erodes. It’s harder to recruit later, and the reputation of the company takes a hit. I’ve seen founders spend more energy fixing cultural scars than improving their product.

This is why I push so hard on GTM clarity first. It protects not just the business, but the people betting their careers on it.
